entry.title: Collection Letters in Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations Complete Understanding
entry.content:
Collection Letters in Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations

Introduction

Collection letters, also known as dunning letters, are formal communications sent to customers with overdue invoices.

These letters follow a predefined sequential process, escalating urgency if payments remain unpaid. Example In D365 F&SCM we need to first post/print Collection letter 1 only after that system will allow to generate Collection letter 2.


Key Benefits of Collection Letters in Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations:

  • Prompt Payment: Encourages customers to pay outstanding invoices on time.
  • Minimum Overdue Balance: Set a minimum overdue balance to automatically generate the collection letter. If overdue is less than minimum overdue balance no collection letter is generated.
  • Fees & Blocking: Optionally apply fees to overdue balances and specify whether to block customer invoicing during letter posting/printing.
  • Customer Relations: Personalise collection letters using electronic reporting or Docentric to enhance customer relationships. The default report format is SSRS, but customisation options are available.
  • Open Transactions: Automatically lists all open transactions for the customer, reducing manual effort.
  • Multiple Collection Letter Levels: Create up to five collection letter levels in Dynamics 365.
  • Automation & Flexibility: Generate, print, and send collection letters with ease, apply interest to overdue balances, and build customised collection letter sequences.

💡 Important:

  • Collection letters follow a sequential process, meaning a 2nd letter cannot be created/posted/printed unless the 1st letter is processed.

Define and Configure a Collection Letter Sequence

A Collection Letter Sequence determines the sequence under which collection letters are sent.

This configuration includes:

Before configuration we need to ask following questions from the business.

  • How many collection letter stages do you need? (like 3 letter or 5 letters)
  • After how many days past the due date should each collection letter be sent? (this will be setup in days column)
  • What fee should be applied at each collection letter stage, and which main account should it post to? (remember only fixed fees can be applied)
  • What should be the payment term for the fees? (the terms of payment section determine the due date for fees charge when posting the collection letter)
  • Do you want to block the customer after processing the collection letter? if yes then at what collection letter stage do you want this setting?

Navigation Path:

📍 Credit and collections > Setup > Set up collection letter sequence

Key Fields in Collection Letter Sequence:

📌 Grace Period Rules:

  • 1st Collection Letter: Grace period is calculated from the invoice due date.
  • 2nd & Subsequent Letters: Grace period is based on the posting or printing date of the previous collection letter (as defined in Accounts Receivable Parameters).

💡 Once created, a Collection Letter Sequence must be mapped to a Posting Profile for the system to generate collection letters.

Assign Collection Letter Sequence to a Posting Profile

The collection letter sequence must be linked to the customer posting profile to ensure correct processing.

Also, in the customer posting profile in the Table restriction fast tab the collection letter toggle should be turned on.

Navigation Path:

📍 Credit and collections > Setup > Customer posting profiles

Configuration Steps:

1️⃣ Go to Credit and Collections > Setup > Customer Posting Profiles.

2️⃣ Expand the Table Restrictions tab and enable Collection Letter Processing.

3️⃣ Under the Setup FastTab, select the appropriate Collection Letter Sequence.

4️⃣ If left blank, collection letters will not be generated for transactions under this posting profile.

📌 Best Practice:

  • Ensure that all posting profiles requiring collection letters have an assigned Collection Letter Sequence.
  • Also note that we do not need to specify collection letter sequence for each of the Account code in the customer posting profile. For example, we do not need to generate collection letter for some groups.

Configure Credit and Collections Parameters

These parameters define how collection letters are generated and processed.

Navigation Path:

📍 Credit and collections > Setup > Accounts receivable parameters

Key Settings:

Process Collection Letters – Create, Review, Print, and Post

The collection letter process in Dynamics 365 F&O consists of two main steps:

  1. Create collection letter
  2. Review and process collection letter

Step 1: Create Collection Letters

📍 Credit and collections > Collection letter > Create collection letters

  • Select the Transaction Types to be included.
  • Choose a posting profile (if different from the default).
  • Apply filters (e.g., specific customers or customer groups) if required.

📌 System Notification:

  • Once created, the system sends a notification under the Action Center.
  • Click Message Details to review the list of generated collection letters.

Note: - In case if you have generated a collection letter number 1 on 14th Feb 2025, and you have provided grace days (let's say 10) in the collection letter sequence page for collection letter number 2, then if you try to run the create collection letter process before 10 days pass from generation of collection letter 1. The system will not generate collection letter.

Step 2: Review, Print, and Post Collection Letters

📍 Credit and collections > Collection letter > Review and process collection letters

  • This screen displays all generated collection letters.
  • Filter by status = Created to view the most recent letters.
  • Click Print > Collection Letter Note to generate the letter layout.
  • The Printed Column will update to Yes once printed.
  • Posting is required, even if no collection fees are charged.

We can also print the collection letter (once we click print button the status of collection letter will be changed to printed)

Once more demonstration

I cancelled the collection letter 2 and its status was changed to cancelled, now I run the create collection letter process again and in this case collection letter 2 will be generated again and not the collection letter 3. Relax! this is system default behaviour.

📌 Important System Behaviour:

✔ If a user cancels a collection letter manually, the status will change to "Cancelled."

✔ The collection letter number remains the same until it is posted / printed (depends on collection parameters). If recreated before posting, it simply replaces the previous version.

✔ Fees configured in the Collection Letter Sequence are only posted when the letter is posted (not when it is created or printed).

✔ The Voucher button is only enabled when a posted collection letter has associated fees.

Batch Process to Auto Post Collection Letter

Once you click on the post button for a collection letter we see "Post collection letter note" pane enabled.

We can check the use run date as posting date and clear the filter (or use appropriate filter on customer account and collection letter based on your requirement)

Posting a collection letter is very crucial and can be very delicate in case fees are also involved. Since, in cases customer pay you the outstanding then you might want to remove the fees, and you need to pass manual entries to remove the posted fees)

Hence in the above case I selected collection letter 1 as criteria (assume there is no fee for this letter)

Setup the recurrence and enabled the batch process toggle to auto post the collection letter using batch process.

Now you are good to go.



Content is for educational purpose please perform your own testing and due diligence before relying on any of the content.

Deep Dive into Collection Letter Code Generation in D365

In my previous part of this blog, we explored how to set up collection letters in Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations (D365).

Now, let’s take a deeper dive into how the system generates collection letter codes. Understanding this process is crucial to ensure that your collection process runs smoothly.

Overview of Collection Letter Codes

In D365, you can generate up to five collection letter codes for a single transaction or customer. Each collection letter generated is assigned a code ranging from 1 to 5. While the current system limits you to five codes, future updates may expand this capability.

For now, let’s focus on how these codes are generated and what factors influence their creation.

Collection Letter Generation: Per Transaction vs. Per Customer

When setting up collection letters, you have the option to generate them either per transaction or per customer. The choice you make here will determine how the system assigns collection letter codes.

  • Per Transaction: Each transaction is treated independently, and collection letters are generated based on the individual past due transaction (Invoice).
  • Per Customer: Collection letters are generated at the customer level, taking into account all open and past due transactions (Invoices) for that customer.
  • This approach (Per Customer) raises an important question: 

How does the system determine the collection letter code when there are multiple transactions, more particularly whether the system takes the oldest past due transaction collection letter code, or it takes the highest collection letter code of all past due transitions and create the next code?
We will discuss this question in this blog with test scenario

  • In the Below Setup we have setup system to create collection letter per customer (it means all open and past due invoices for a customer will be available in a single collection letter). We have also setup "Update collection letter code" to Posting, it means until and unless we post a collection letter code the new code will not be generated.

How the System Determines Collection Letter Codes

To understand how the system generates collection letter codes, let’s walk through an example.

Example Scenario

Consider the collection letter setup

Consider the following two invoices for a single customer:

Qns: How did I managed to create collection letter code #2 even if we can see that for the oldest invoice (#1) we have collection letter code #1 only.
Ans: I generated collection letter #1 for both, then I changed the due date of oldest invoice to future date, so it was not past due then I run the create collection letter again. Hence in second run the collection letter generated has only the invoice #2 and collection letter code for invoice #2 was updated to 2. Then I changed the due date of Invoice #1 to 2-Feb-2025.

Current system date is 22-Feb-2025

First invoice is oldest invoice with due date of 2nd Feb and the second invoice is due for 12th-Feb-2025.

The Last Collection Letter Code Column determines the Collection letter code issued for a particular transaction.

  • For Invoice 1 last collection letter code is #1
  • For Invoice 2 last collection letter code is #2

Question: - The next collection letter code the be generated when we run the "Create Collection Letter Code" process should be?

Answer: - The next collection letter code will be based on the highest collection letter code generated among all the past due transaction. We will check this in the test scenario in this blog.

Read the below Note to Understand about the transaction level collection letter code.

Note: -
Even if we have setup system to create collection letter per customer still for each transaction the code will be update and we can check that code in the Review and Post Collection Letter > Select the collection letter > Transactions.

In case of "Create Collection letter per customer" the highest collection letter code among all the transaction become the collection letter code for the transaction and the collection fees as determined based on that code only.

In case of "Create Collection letter per transaction" the transaction level code becomes the collection letter code hence there is no question about how system choose the collection letter.

Now let's proceed with the scenario

In this scenario, we have two invoices with different due dates and days past due.

The system needs to determine the next collection letter code based on these transactions.

Step 1 - Posting Collection Letter #1

When generating the first collection letter, the system will consider the following:

  • Invoice 1: Due on 2-Feb-25, 20 days past due, with a last collection letter code of 1.
  • Invoice 2: Due on 12-Feb-25, 10 days past due, with a last collection letter code of 1.

The system will generate Collection Letter #1 for both invoices.


After generating Collection Letter #1, the system will post the associated fees. In this case, the fees are as follows:

  • Collection Letter #1: INR 20

The collection letter date is set to 22-Feb-25, but the due date for the fees is 23-Feb-25, based on the payment term defined in the collection letter sequence (Net 1 day) for the fees (Check previous blog to understand more).

Voucher of Fees Posted:

Step 2 - Posting Collection Letter #2

Now, let’s assume we change the due date of Invoice #1 to a future date and re-run the collection letter creation process. The system will now generate Collection Letter #2 for Invoice #2.

Also notice the fees posted. Hence in case even if collection letter #1 has fees higher than collection letter 2 but still the fees for collection letter 2 will be posted. Since collection letter 2 is issued in the case below.

We can see that collection letter is generated for Invoice #2 only.

After posting Collection Letter #2, we have the following status:

  • Invoice 1: Collection Letter Code 1 generated.
  • Invoice 2: Collection Letter Codes 1 and 2 generated.

Step 3 - Posting Collection Letter #3

Now If we re-run the process again how will the system determine the collection letter code. There are two possible outcomes:

  1. If the next code is 3: This means the system is considering the highest code from all open transactions.
  2. If the next code is 2: This means the system is considering the highest code from the oldest invoice (based on due date).

As we can see that collection letter code generated is Collection letter 3 (In Identification section)

Hence the collection letter code for next letter will be the highest code among all the past due transactions included in that letter.

I hope this blog provides a clear understanding of how collection letter codes are generated in D365.

If you have any questions or need further clarification, feel free to reach out in the comments section below!

Signing off

Manu Sharma

entry.title: Understanding the Production Posting Profiles
entry.content:
In D365 F&O, production accounting follows a "Physical" vs. "Financial" update logic. Temporary "Estimated" entries are posted during the process and are fully reversed and replaced by "Actual" entries when the production order is Ended. 1. Material and Route Consumption (The WIP Phase) When you post a Picking List (Materials) or a Route Card (Labor/Machine time), D365 records the value of these resources in Work in Progress (WIP) accounts. Material Consumption ($25,550,000): This represents the raw materials taken from the warehouse and moved into the production floor. Route Consumption ($5,250,000): This is the cost of labor or machine hours applied. Debit 150200 (WIP-Labor): Increases the value of the "unfinished" product. Credit 600500 (Direct Labor Applied): This is an Absorption Account. It offsets the payroll expenses already recorded in the General Ledger, showing that the labor was "absorbed" into a product rather than just being a period expense. 2. Report as Finished (The Physical Phase) The Report as Finished (RAF) stage signifies that the items are physically complete and sitting in the Finished Goods (FG) warehouse, even though the final "Financial" cost hasn't been locked in yet. Debit 140200 (Finished Goods Inventory): Increases inventory at an Estimated cost (usually based on the BOM/Route estimation or standard cost). Credit 150150 (Production WIP): Reduces the WIP account, moving the value out of "Work in Progress" and into "Finished Goods." Amount $30,200,750: This is your total estimated manufactured cost (Materials + Labor + Indirects). 3. Indirect Costs ($200,750) These are overheads (e.g., electricity, depreciation, or rent) calculated via the Costing Sheet. The system uses Estimated indirect cost absorbed (600510) as an offset to pull these "invisible" costs into the product's value. 4. Production Control / Ending (The Settlement Phase) The voucher PCV-14187 is the most critical. It occurs when you change the production order status to Ended. This process performs three main actions: Reverses all Physical/Estimated entries: You see $30,200,750 being credited back out of FG Inventory to "clear the slate." Clears WIP: All temporary WIP accounts (150150, 150200, 150250) are zeroed out. Posts Final Financial Cost: The system calculates the Actual cost ($31,000,750). Why is there a difference? Estimated Cost: $30,200,750 Final Cost accounted: $31,000,750 Analysis: The $800,000 difference is a Production Variance. This happens if you consumed more material than planned, if labor took longer, or if the unit price of raw materials changed between the time you started and finished the order. 1. The Root Cause: Material Usage Variance The entire $800,000 variance comes from a single raw material: MS-RM-101 (Cost Group: RM-RAM). Estimated Consumption: 1,000 units Realized Consumption: 1,050 units Variance in Quantity: 50 units (Over-consumption) Because the unit price for this item is $16,000 ($16,000,000 ÷ 1,000), the 50 extra units consumed resulted in an additional cost of $800,000. In Dynamics 365, this is classified as a Quantity Variance or Usage Variance. It suggests that the production process was less efficient than planned for this specific component—perhaps due to scrap, rework, or a calculation error in the BOM. The Picking List is where the $800,000 "leakage" occurred. In D365 F&O, this journal records the physical movement of raw materials from the warehouse to WIP.
The Culprit (MS-RM-101): * The Plan: 1,000 units at $16,000/unit. The Reality: 1,050 units were "picked" and posted. Financial Impact: As soon as this journal was posted, the system debited WIP-Materials (150150) for $16.8M instead of the estimated $16M. The Others: Items MS-RM-102 through MS-RM-105 were posted exactly at their estimated quantities. 2. Areas of Zero Variance It is equally important to note the areas where the production was perfectly aligned with the estimate: Other Materials: Items MS-RM-102 through MS-RM-105 had zero variance. The realized consumption and costs exactly matched the estimates. Route/Labor Efficiency: * OP-ASS (Assembly): Took exactly the 50 hours estimated. OP-PCK (Packing): Took exactly the 25 hours estimated. Since the hours and the hourly rates matched, there was no Substitution or Efficiency Variance for labor. Indirect Costs (Overheads): Electricity and Machine Depreciation were "Output unit based." Since the final good quantity (500 pcs) matched the estimated quantity, these overheads were applied exactly as planned.
For auditors, having a clear, documented breakdown of why a $30.2M estimate became a $31M actual cost is crucial. Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations provides specific tools to extract this exact "Standard vs. Realized" comparison. Here is how you can pull these details, offering both a quick on-screen analysis and a formal report for your audit trail. Method 1: The Quick On-Screen View (Best for Ad-Hoc Analysis) Before running a full report, you can view the exact breakdown directly on the production order. This is typically the fastest way to investigate a variance before answering auditor questions. Navigate to Production control > Production orders > All production orders. Select your specific production order (e.g., PRO-001648). On the Action Pane, go to the Manage costs tab. In the Costing group, click on View calculation details. Select the Overview costing tab. What you will see: This form provides a side-by-side grid of Estimated consumption/cost versus Realized consumption/cost. If you filter this grid by your specific Cost Group (e.g., RM-RAM), the $800,000 variance for the 50 extra units of MS-RM-101 will be immediately visible and highlighted. Method 2: The "Cost Estimates and Costing" Report (Best for Auditors) When auditors request a formal document showing the financial settlement of the production order, this is the standard report to generate. Navigation: Go to Production control > Inquiries and reports > Costing > Cost estimates and costing. Recommended Parameter Setup: When the report dialog opens, set the following parameters to ensure the data is clean and focused: Records to include: Click Filter and set the Production field to your specific order number (PRO-001648). Level of detail: Set to Item and resource (or Cost group if the auditors prefer to see it summarized by Material vs. Labor vs. Overhead). Include estimated cost: Yes (This is your $30,200,750 baseline). Include realized cost: Yes (This is your $31,000,750 actual). Show variances: Yes (This forces the report to calculate and display the exact delta column). How to Guide the Auditors Through the Report When you hand this PDF to the auditors, you can direct their attention to how the system classifies the variance: The Baseline: Show them the Estimated Cost column matching the $30,200,750 originally posted to Finished Goods (Account 140200) during the "Report as Finished" stage. The Variance: Point them to the specific line for item MS-RM-101. The report will clearly show a Quantity Variance of 50 units, resulting in an unfavorable cost variance of $800,000. The Settlement: Explain that voucher PCV-14187 (from your initial data) is the financial result of this exact report. The system took the total realized cost ($31,000,750) and used it to reverse the estimates and settle the Work in Progress (WIP) accounts to zero. By providing both the posting profile extraction and this specific variance report, your auditors will have a complete, traceable map of the entire $31M production cycle.

entry.title: Create Demo MT940 and Test Advance Bank Reconciliation
entry.content:
Decoding the MT940 Bank Statement for D365 Advanced Bank Reconciliation

While ISO 20022 CAMT.053 is rapidly becoming the gold standard for global banking communication, the classic SWIFT MT940 format remains a powerful and ubiquitous staple for automated bank reconciliation. 

Understanding how to read an MT940 file—and how Dynamics 365 Finance interprets its structured tags—is an essential skill for any financial implementation team.

Unlike the highly nested XML structure of CAMT.053, MT940 is a "flat-file" standard established by SWIFT. It relies on sequential alphanumeric tags to denote fields. If a bank omits a mandatory tag or misformats a string, the D365 import process will likely fail.

Let's break down the core architecture of an MT940 statement and highlight the critical fields required for a seamless D365 Finance integration.

The Anatomy of an MT940 Statement

An MT940 file systematically structures its data into specific blocks marked by tags. A tag starts with a colon, followed by the tag number, and ends with another colon (e.g., :25:).

Here are the most critical tags you need to understand when configuring your D365 Bank Account Master and Advanced Bank Reconciliation Matching Rules:

1. Tag :20: - Transaction Reference Number (TRN)

  • What it is: The unique reference number assigned to the statement message by the sender.
  • D365 Impact: D365 uses this for internal tracking and duplicate prevention. If an MT940 file is imported twice, D365 checks this reference, alongside the statement date and number, to block duplicate imports.

2. Tag :25: - Account Identification [CRITICAL FOR MATCHING]

  • What it is: This identifies your bank account. It is usually represented as the IBAN or the standard domestic bank account number.
  • D365 Impact: This is arguably the most crucial tag for the import process. The standard D365 MT940 parser looks at Tag :25: to match the statement block to the internal D365 Bank Account.
  • The Rule: The IBAN field or the Bank account number field on your D365 Bank Account Master must be an exact alphanumeric match to the contents of Tag :25:.

3. Tag :28C: - Statement Number / Sequence Number

  • What it is: A progressive number that indicates the chronological sequence of the statements (e.g., 15/1 indicating Statement 15, page 1).
  • D365 Impact: Helps D365 chronologically sequence the statement headers in the Advanced Bank Reconciliation worksheet.

4. Tags :60F: / :60M: - Opening Balance

  • What it is: The opening balance of the account at the start of the statement period. F stands for First/Opening, M indicates an intermediate balance.
  • Structure: It packs multiple data points into a single string. It starts with C (Credit) or D (Debit), followed by the Date (YYMMDD), Currency (EUR), and Amount (15000,00).
  • D365 Impact: D365 uses the currency defined here to validate against the D365 Bank Account Master base currency. If the currencies clash, the import will be blocked. The opening balance is also verified mathematically against the sum of the transactions to authenticate the file.

5. Tag :61: - Statement Line (The Transaction details) [CRITICAL FOR MATCHING]

  • What it is: The meat of the file. Every single financial transaction has its own Tag :61:.
  • Structure Example: 61:2603310331CR1500,00NMSCNONREF
  • Breakdown: Let's tear this string apart because it drives your D365 transaction lines:
    • 260331: Value date (YYMMDD) - March 31, 2026
    • 0331: Entry date (MMDD)
    • C / D / CR / RC: Credit or Debit indicators (R usually denotes a Reversal). This dictates whether D365 writes a positive or negative amount.
    • 1500,00: Transaction Amount.
    • NMSC: SWIFT Transaction Type Identifier Code (e.g., NMSC for Misc, NTRF for Transfer, NCHG for Charges).
    • NONREF: Bank Reference.
  • D365 Impact: D365 Matching Rules heavily leverage the SWIFT Transaction Code (the 4 letters like NMSC). You can instruct D365: "If the line is a Debit and the Bank transaction code is NCHG, bypass the subledger and automatically post this to the Bank Fees General Ledger account."

6. Tag :86: - Information to Account Owner [CRITICAL FOR CLEARING]

  • What it is: Directly follows a Tag :61: line. This is the Remittance Information block. It contains unformatted metadata regarding who paid you and why, like Invoice Numbers, Vendor Names, or payment descriptions.
  • D365 Impact: This is the playground for D365 Advanced Bank Reconciliation's more complex features. Because the tag often contains a massive, unstructured string of text, you utilize Matching Rules to scan the :86: tag. If a customer paid Invoice INV-90921, the text INV-90921 will live inside this tag. D365 searches this block, pulls the invoice ID, and uses it to auto-settle the open Accounts Receivable balance.

7. Tags :62F: / :62M: - Closing Balance

  • What it is: The ending check-figure. Functions identically to Tag :60F:.
  • D365 Impact: D365 validates the imported data by taking the Opening Balance (:60F:), netting all the Tag :61: lines, and verifying that the final number perfectly matches Tag :62F:. If it's off by even a penny, the statement is typically flagged as structurally invalid and won't reconcile.

Summary

For D365 implementations, the MT940 format thrives in its standardized rigidity. Ensure that the Account Identification (Tag :25:) perfectly aligns with the IBAN in D365, and heavily utilize the SWIFT Action codes in Tag :61: and the dense text inside Tag :86: to automate your daily transaction matching.

In complex food manufacturing, products are rarely made in a single, uninterrupted step. Instead, production is broken down into intermediate stages using Semi-Finished Goods (SFGs). This allows a business to accurately track the cost, yield, and inventory of intermediate items—like dough or bulk sauces—before they are consumed into the final retail packaging.

Financial Impact: When this batch is started, the system debits WIP for the flour and water. As the industrial mixers run, labor and overhead costs are "absorbed" into WIP. When this first batch order is Ended, the total accumulated cost ($2,600.00) is credited out of WIP and debited into our SFG Inventory account. entry.title: Automatic Posting of Approved Jorunals (AP, AR, GL, FA etc)
entry.content:
Work Smarter: Automating Your General Ledger Posting in D365 F&O

In the fast-paced world of finance, every click counts. If you’re using Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations (D365 F&O), you know the drill: an accountant enters a journal, a manager approves the workflow, and then... it just sits there. Someone still has to go back in and manually click "Post."

Why? It’s time to let the system finish what it started. 

By automating the posting of approved journals, you minimize human error, ensure your books are up-to-the-minute accurate, and free your team for more strategic work.

The Setup: How to Automate Your Posting

To turn on the "auto-pilot" for your Daily Journals, follow these navigation steps within D365:

1. Define Your Filter Logic

Navigate to General Ledger > Journal Entries > Post Journals. Once there, click Select and set these specific filters:

  • Posted: Set to No

  • Journal Type: Set to Daily (General Journals)

  • Workflow Approval Status: Change the field selection to Approved.

2. Configure the Automation

Once your filters are set, you need to tell the system to run this search on a loop:

  1. Click Run in the background.

  2. Click Recurrence > Select No End Date.

  3. Choose your Recurrence Pattern (e.g., every 30 minutes or at the end of every day).

  4. Set Batch Processing to Yes.

  5. CRITICAL: Set Late Selection to Yes.

  6. Click OK.

A notification will appear confirming the batch has been added to the queue. You're officially automated!

Deep Dive: Why These Settings Matter

Setting up the batch job is easy, but understanding why we choose certain toggles is what separates a user from an expert. 

Let’s look at the two most common questions regarding this setup.

What exactly is "Late Selection" and why do I need it?

Think of Late Selection as the difference between a "one-time list" and a "permanent rule."

  • Standard Selection: The system looks for approved journals right now, makes a list of their IDs, and saves that list. Every time the batch runs, it only looks for those specific IDs. Since they’ll be posted after the first run, the batch job will never find anything new to do.

  • Late Selection (The Expert Choice): Instead of saving a list of journals, the system saves the query. Every time the batch job wakes up, it re-scans the entire system for newly approved journals that weren't there before.

The takeaway: Without Late Selection, your automation isn't actually automatic—it's just a scheduled attempt to do the same task over and over.

Why is the "Workflow Approval" filter so important?

You might be tempted to just tell the system to "Post everything that isn't posted." Don't. Adding the Workflow approval status = Approved filter is your primary safety valve for three reasons:

  1. Segregation of Duties: It ensures that no transaction hits your General Ledger without being vetted by an authorized person. This is essential for SOX compliance and internal audits.

  2. Preventing System "Noise": If the system tries to post a journal that is still in "Draft" or "In Review," the batch job will fail and throw an error. If you have 50 journals in progress, your error logs will be a nightmare to read.

  3. Accuracy: It prevents half-finished journals from accidentally impacting your financial reporting.

Final Thoughts

Automation isn't just about speed; it's about control. 

By combining the power of D365 batch jobs with smart filters, you create a seamless, hands-off process that respects your business's internal controls.

Master the Dunning Process: A Step-by-Step Guide to Collection Letters in Dynamics 365 Finance

1. Introduction: The Strategic Role of Collection Management

Effective collection management is the lifeblood of organizational liquidity, directly impacting the optimization of working capital and cash flow predictability. In Dynamics 365 Finance, Collection Letters—historically known as "dunning letters"—serve as a formal, sequential escalation tool designed to recover overdue balances while preserving professional customer relationships. These letters are not merely alerts; they are a structured communication path where the system enforces a mandatory sequence (e.g., Letter 1 must be processed before Letter 2).

This automated logic ensures a professional escalation path, preventing administrative gaps and providing a defensible audit trail of collection efforts. While the standard SSRS report format is functional, a Senior Solutions Architect will often recommend utilizing Electronic Reporting or third-party enhancements like Docentric to achieve the high degree of personalization and professional branding required for effective dunning communications. The transition from configuration to execution begins with defining the "brain" of the logic: the collection letter sequence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Phase I: Architectural Configuration of the Collection Sequence

The Collection Letter Sequence determines the timing, financial penalties, and severity of each communication level. It is the core framework that prevents a customer from receiving a legal warning before a gentle reminder.

To configure the sequence, navigate to: Credit and collections > Setup > Set up collection letter sequence.

Collection Letter Code
Description
Days / Grace Period
Fees & Main Account
Terms of Payment
Level 1
Gentle Reminder
Calculated from the invoice due date.
Usually no fee; polite notice.
N/A
Level 2
Formal Reminder
Based on previous letter's Post/Print date.
Fixed fee; mapped to Main Account.
Terms of Payment for the fee.
Level 3
Warning Letter
Based on previous letter's Post/Print date.
Increased fee; higher urgency.
Terms of Payment for the fee.
Level 4/5
Final Notice / Legal
Based on previous letter's Post/Print date.
Maximum fee; triggers Block.
Terms of Payment for the fee.

Strategic Blocking & Fees: The Block toggle is a critical control. When enabled (typically at Level 4 or 5), the system automatically updates the Invoice and delivery on hold field on the customer record to Invoice. This prevents further credit exposure while the account is in legal review. Furthermore, the Terms of Payment assigned in the sequence setup are vital; they determine the specific due date for the collection fees once the letter is posted.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. Phase II: Mapping and Parameter Synchronization

The Posting Profile acts as the bridge between the collection logic and the General Ledger, ensuring that all fees and letter statuses are recorded against the correct financial dimensions.

  • Posting Profile Integration: Navigate to Credit and collections > Setup > Customer posting profiles. Under the Table Restrictions FastTab, the Collection Letter toggle must be enabled. Then, map the specific Collection Letter Sequence in the Setup FastTab.
  • Parameter Optimization: Navigate to Credit and collections > Setup > Accounts receivable parameters. In the Collections tab, you must define if the "next" letter is triggered by Posting or Printing.
The "So What?" Layer: Choosing between Customer vs. Transaction generation levels is a strategic decision. Generating "per customer" reduces administrative bloat by consolidating all overdue invoices into a single notice. "Per transaction" is only recommended for specialized industries where individual invoices represent distinct contracts with separate legal escalation requirements.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

4. Phase III: The Execution Lifecycle—Create, Review, and Post

The operational flow follows a strict "Create-Review-Process" lifecycle to safeguard customer relationships against automated errors.

  1. Generation: Navigate to Credit and collections > Collection letter > Create collection letters. Users apply filters by Customer pool or Transaction type. Note that the system strictly enforces grace periods; Level 2 will not generate if the required days have not passed since Level 1.
  2. Review and Printing: Navigate to Credit and collections > Collection letter > Review and process collection letters. Here, letters remain in Created status for agent review.
  3. Financial Posting: Posting is mandatory to move a customer to the next level in the sequence, regardless of whether fees are applied. Once posted, the Voucher button enables an audit of the ledger impact for associated fees.
The "So What?" Layer: System behavior during cancellations is designed for audit integrity. If a user cancels a "Level 2" letter, the system resets to that level for the next run, ensuring no steps are skipped. Crucially, the Collection letter number remains the same until the letter is posted or printed, maintaining a clear audit trail of the document's lifecycle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

5. Phase IV: Advanced Automation and Process Hierarchies

High-volume environments should move from manual runs to Collection Process Automation, allowing for complex strategies based on customer segments.

Strategy-Based Approach: In the Process Hierarchy (found via Credit and collections > Setup > Process automation > Collection process setup), you define Pool IDs to target specific segments. This is also where you configure Quiet Days—a parameter that prevents over-communication by ensuring a set interval passes before another automated action occurs.

Automated Action Types:

  1. Collection Letters: Automates the traditional 1-5 sequence.
  2. Email Notifications: Ideal for "Pre-dunning" (e.g., 2 days before the due date). Strategic tip: Emails can be routed to the Business contact type for customers or even the Sales Team for internal accountability and follow-up.
  3. Collection Activities: Generates internal tasks (e.g., phone calls) for agents.
Personalization via Templates: Utilize Email template map setup to define placeholders. This allows dynamic data such as Customer account, Invoice amount, and Invoice number to be inserted into automated emails, providing a personalized touch despite the automation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

6. Phase V: Handling Escalations—Interest Notes and Write-Offs

When standard dunning fails, the lifecycle moves to financial penalties or balance relief.

Interest Notes: Interest codes determine how to charge for the "cost" of delayed payments.

  • Single Rate: A flat percentage.
  • Multiple Rates: A stepped deterrent (e.g., 1.5% for 0–30 days, increasing to 2.5% for 61+ days). Architect’s Recommendation: Use Multiple Rates for chronic late-payers to mirror the increasing administrative and legal costs as debt ages.
  • Closed Transactions: A high-value insight is calculating interest on closed transactions. This captures interest for the period an invoice was late after it was paid but before the interest note was run.
The Write-Off Process: Navigate to Credit and collections > Collections > Aged balances and use the Write-off function for uncollectible debt. The "So What?" Layer: Write-offs represent a direct hit to the P&L. Dynamics 365 uses Reason Codes mapped to Bad Debt Expense accounts to ensure a robust audit trail, ensuring every write-off is categorized correctly for financial audits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

7. Conclusion: Reporting and Strategic Oversight

A collection strategy is only as effective as the data driving it. To maintain oversight, the Customer aging snapshot must be run periodically to populate the Aged balances list page.

Key Reporting Criteria for Leadership:

  • Aging as of: Defines the bucket placement.
  • Balance as of: The transaction cutoff date.
  • Criteria: Selection of Transaction date vs. Due date.
  • Printing Direction: Use Forward for cash flow forecasting and Backward for historical delinquency analysis.

By unifying architectural configuration, sequential execution, and process automation, Dynamics 365 Finance empowers organizations to maintain a healthy cash position while minimizing the manual overhead of debt recovery.

entry.title: Bank Master Setup
entry.content:
Demystifying D365 Finance Bank Master Setup for CAMT.053 Advanced Bank Reconciliation

When implementing Advanced Bank Reconciliation in Dynamics 365 Finance using the standardized ISO 20022 CAMT.053 format, the configuration of your Bank account master data is the ultimate linchpin. 

You can perfect your Electronic Reporting framework and painstakingly design your matching rules, but if the foundational bank account identifiers are incorrect, your statements will fail to import or map correctly.

In this deep dive, we will break down every field you see on the D365 Finance Bank Account Master page, explaining what it does and—crucially—whether and how the standard CAMT.053 import process cares about it.

1. Bank Account Header: The Primary Identifiers

This section contains the most visible characteristics of your bank account. These fields are vital because the system uses them to match the incoming XML file to the correct internal D365 record.

  • Bank account: This is the unique internal D365 identifier (Primary Key) for the bank account record. While it's critical for D365, the CAMT.053 file never contains this internal identifier.

  • Bank account number: [CRITICAL FOR CAMT.053] This is your actual, real-world bank account number. If your bank does not utilize IBANs (e.g., in the US or Canada), the Electronic Reporting (ER) import configuration will usually scan the <Acct><Id><Othr><Id> node within the CAMT.053 XML to find this exact string. It must be an identical match (no extra dashes, spaces, or leading zeros unless they are also in the XML file).

  • Routing number type & Routing number: These identify the bank branch itself (e.g., ABA in the US, Transit Number in Canada). While more crucial for outbound payments (ACH/Wires), some bespoke CAMT.053 files bundle the routing number with the account number. If this happens, your standard ER import might fail to identify the account, requiring a specialized mapping to strip the routing number out before matching.

  • Name, Company statement name, Destination name: These are largely reference fields. D365 uses them to populate reports, screens, and vendor/customer payment references. The CAMT.053 file does contain account names (usually under <Nm>), but standard D365 does not use the name to identify the account during import—it relies strictly on the structured alphanumeric IDs (IBAN/Account Number).

2. Internal Information & Currency

This section ties the bank subledger to your General Ledger and dictates transaction currencies.

  • Main account: The GL account where all transactions will be posted. When you post a reconciled bank statement, the offset transactions (like bank fees or interest marked during reconciliation) are driven by matching rules, but the core balance hits this Main account.

  • Accounting / Reporting currency exchange rate type: Determines which exchange rate table is used to revalue foreign currency bank balances at month-end.

  • Currency: [CRITICAL FOR CAMT.053] The base currency of the bank account. The CAMT.053 file declares a currency for opening and closing balances explicitly (e.g., <Amt Ccy="EUR">). If a file arrives with balances in EUR, but this field in D365 is set to USD, the system will throw validation errors and refuse to process the statement lines predictably.

  • Allow transactions in additional currency: If toggled to 'Yes', you can post D365 transactions to this account in a foreign currency. However, standard CAMT.053 files are almost always reported in a single, fixed ledger currency per statement.

3. Account Active Status & Bank Account Status

  • Active from / Active to & Bank account status: Standard lifecycle management. If a bank account is flagged as "Inactive" or the statement date in the CAMT.053 file falls outside of the active date parameters, D365 will prevent you from importing statements or posting reconciliations against that account.

  • Credit limit: A soft/hard limit for your Bank Balance.

4. Positive Pay Format

  • Format & Positive pay start date: [NOT USED IN CAMT.053] Positive pay is an outbound fraud-prevention process where you send a file to the bank listing all the checks you have issued so the bank knows what to honor. This section has absolutely zero impact on incoming bank reconciliations.

5. Additional Identification: The Global Matrix

This section expands globally to accommodate localized bank identifiers. The CAMT.053 is an international ISO 20022 standard, but European implementations rely heavily on these fields—specifically the IBAN and SWIFT code.

The Heavyweights: 

* IBAN (International Bank Account Number): [THE HOLY GRAIL FOR CAMT.053] If you are operating in Europe, the Middle East, or anywhere IBAN is adopted, this field is mandatory. The CAMT.053 ER framework is pre-wired to look explicitly at the <Acct><Id><IBAN> tag. 

If this tag is present, D365 will use the IBAN to instantly link the XML statement to the correct D365 bank account, bypassing the local "Bank account number". 

* SWIFT code (BIC): [HIGHLY IMPORTANT] Found under the <FinInstnId><BIC> or <BICFI> tag in the XML file, this identifies the financial institution routing the data. Some banks require strict validation, and ensuring the SWIFT code matches your bank master ensures the statement passes initial structural validations.

The Regional Specifics: The rest of these fields are highly localized. While they are pivotal for outgoing payments (Pain.001) or Direct Debits (Pain.008), they are vastly ignored by the standard CAMT.053 (statement import) simply because the IBAN or standard Account Number is sufficient to verify whose account the statement belongs to. 

 * CH (Switzerland) & LI (Liechtenstein): * ESR / BESR ID number / Post account: Historical Swiss payment slips. * Fee ESR account number / Post fee: Used for routing specific postal charges. * QR-IBAN: The modern Swiss QR-bill identifier, replacing ESR. * UK & Commonwealth: * Sort code: The British 6-digit bank routing number. * Miscellaneous: * CIN, Company ID, Division: Often used for corporate identifier mapping in direct debits (e.g., SEPA Creditor ID). * Clearing / Interbank clearing code: Localized domestic clearing numbers (e.g., German BLZ). * Direct debit ID: Your organization's ID for initiating pull payments.

Note on Localized fields and CAMT.053: Occasionally, a bank's CAMT.053 file might embed localized payment references in the statement lines (for example, to recognize a batch of paid ESR/QR invoices). When this happens, matching rules are configured to parse the <Ustrd> (Unstructured Remittance) or <Strd> (Structured Remittance) tags to find these IDs, but the import framework does not use them at the header level to identify the bank account itself.

Summary: The CAMT.053 Setup Checklist

To summarize, if your goal is purely to ensure a CAMT.053 file imports successfully and finds the right bank account for reconciliation, focus on achieving perfect alignment in these three areas: 1. IBAN: If the bank provides it in the XML, make sure it is populated in D365 with no spaces. 2. Bank account number: If IBAN is not utilized, ensure this exactly mirrors the string provided in the <Othr><Id> node of the bank's file. 3. Currency: Ensure the ISO currency code matches the statement currency precisely.

Everything else ensures your general ledger balances properly and allows your outgoing payments to function, but these three are the absolute gatekeepers for incoming advanced bank reconciliations.

Beyond the Basics: Understanding "Enterprise-Grade" CAMT.053 Structures

When you download a CAMT.053 file from a global Tier-1 bank (like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, or Citi), you will often encounter an "Enterprise-Grade" highly verbose XML structure. While a basic CAMT.053 file only needs account numbers, dates, and amounts to clear standard D365 matching, these advanced elements provide granular auditing and automated statement clearing capabilities.

Here is a breakdown of the advanced XML structures you should understand when building or troubleshooting robust D365 imported statements:

1. The Transaction Summary Block (<TxsSummry>)

  • Where it lives: At the bottom of the <Stmt> block, just before the transaction rows begin.
  • What it does: Contains <TtlNtries>, <TtlCdtNtries>, and <TtlDbtNtries>. It acts as a mathematical checksum for the statement, defining exactly how many credits and debits the ERP should expect to process in the file, and what their sum should be.
  • D365 Impact: While D365 is usually lenient if this block is missing (as long as opening and closing balances calculate correctly), strict localizations or enterprise parsers will use it to reject incomplete files instantly.

2. ISO Transaction Families (<BkTxCd>)

  • Where it lives: Inside each <Ntry> (transaction row).
  • What it does: Instead of a simple proprietary text code (like Fee or Wire), the Enterprise standard lists a <Domn> (Domain), <Fmly> (Family), and <SubFmlyCd> (Sub-Family). For example, Domain: PMNT (Payment), Family: ICDT (Issued Credit Transfer).
  • D365 Impact: You can configure Dynamics 365 Advanced Bank Reconciliation Matching Rules to explicitly target these ISO Domains. This allows you to build highly dynamic rules: "If the Domain is PMNT and Family is RCDT (Received Credit Transfer), automatically map this to the Customer Receipts clearing account."

3. Explicit Reversal Indicators (<RvslInd>)

  • Where it lives: At the root of a transaction <Ntry>.
  • What it does: Uses a strict boolean (true or false) to inform the system if the line is a bank correction or reversal. Verbose statements will also include the <RtrInf><Rsn> (Return Info Reason) block deeper in the details to provide the exact banking return code (e.g., R02 for Account Closed).
  • D365 Impact: When importing into D365, Advanced Matching Rules can target the Reversal Indicator. This allows D365 to instantly pair erroneous bank entry debits with their corrective credits, clearing them against each other and bypassing the General Ledger completely without manual intervention.

4. Deep Account Servicer Identification (<Svcr>)

  • Where it lives: Inside the statement <Acct> header.
  • What it does: Defines the <FinInstnId><BIC> (Bank Identifier Code) and the specific Bank's Name (e.g. Goldman Sachs Bank).
  • D365 Impact: Serves as a secondary authentication gate. If the BIC inside the XML statement does not match the SWIFT code loaded into the D365 Bank Master global matrix, the system can flag the file and prevent the user from importing data into the wrong legal entity.

5. Timezone Dateline Issues (The "+05:30" Shift Error)

  • Where it lives: Extensively applied to the <DtTm> nodes in the XML (e.g. 2026-03-31T23:59:59Z).
  • What it does: By ISO 8601 standard, the "Z" appending a timestamp signifies Zulu/UTC time.
  • D365 Impact [CAUTION]: D365 actively translates UTC time into the local user session timezone! If you import a statement with a <ToDtTm> of 2026-03-31T23:59:59Z and your D365 user is configuring the bank rec in Indian Standard Time (UTC+05:30), D365 will display the closing boundary as April 1 (05:29:59 AM). This completely breaks month-end reconciliation groupings because your statement visually "spills" into the next month!
  • The Fix: While you can pad your XML timestamps to mathematically avoid the dateline, the structurally superior method is to use the native D365 functionality during the import process. When clicking Import statement, locate the 'Time zone preference' dropdown. By changing the selection from 'Auto' to 'No conversion', D365 is instructed to respect the raw date string exactly as it is written in the XML, entirely bypassing the local timezone shift!

Important Blogs: - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/dynamics365/release-plan/2023wave2/finance-supply-chain/dynamics365-finance/generate-payment-journal-settle-open-invoices-directly-bank-reconciliation

entry.title: Bank Reconciliation in D365 - Part 1 - End to End Manual Bank Reconciliation
entry.content:
Bank Reconciliation is a periodic process which helps to Match the Bank Account balance as per the ERP (books of accounts) with the Balance as per the Bank.

Why the difference arises?

First Category of Differences - There are possibility that some of the transactions that are entered in the bank are not entered in the ERP for example

1. A customer deposited money in the bank but did not inform the ERP team of our (let's say USMF) company.

2. Dividend from subsidiary credited to the bank but the ERP team missed to enter in the Books of accounts

3. Some Charges / Interest charged by the Bank but not entered in the ERP.

Second Category of Differences - There are possibility that some of the transactions are entered by the ERP team but those are not entered in the Bank for example

1. Customer check Deposited to Bank but was not cleared.

2. We issued check to vendor on 31st March but vendor submitted and get it cleared on 1st April.

Bank reconciliation helps us to manage these differences.


There are some questions which used to come into my mind when I used to prepare the Bank Reconciliation.

Qns 1. When preparing the bank statement if we found some transaction which get cleared in next period for example vendor was issued check (as discussed above) then should we reverse the transaction and report it again in the next period to make the balance of the bank matching with the books of accounts (ERP Balance).

Ans 1. 

Reversing an outstanding check and re-posting it in the next month is not the correct accounting practice. Doing so would misrepresent your financial position, distort vendor aging, and create audit trails that are difficult to defend.

Here is the breakdown of why this shouldn't be reversed and how the accounting logic works in Dynamics 365 Finance.

1. Why You Should Never "Reverse and Re-post"

  • Accuracy of Dates: Accounting rules require you to record a payment on the day the check is issued (the day you no longer have control over those funds). If you wrote the check on March 30, it must be recorded in March.

  • Vendor Aging: If you reverse the check on March 31, the vendor invoice will suddenly appear "unpaid" on your March financial reports, even though you have already sent the payment.

  • Audit Trail: Reversing a valid payment simply to make a reconciliation screen "match" creates "noise" in the ledger. Auditors look for "reversals" as potential red flags for fraud or error correction.

2. The Accounting Flow

When you post a check in D365, the following happens immediately in the General Ledger:

AccountDebitCredit
Vendor Summary Account (Accounts Payable)$1,000
Bank Main Account (Asset)$1,000

At this moment, your Book Balance (the balance in D365) has decreased. However, your Bank Balance (the money actually in the bank) will not decrease until the vendor deposits that check and the bank processes it.

3. How the Reconciliation Handles the Difference

The purpose of a Bank Reconciliation is not to make the Book Balance match the Statement Balance on the ledger; it is to explain the difference between the two.

In the Manual (Simple) Bank Reconciliation form in D365:

  1. Statement Ending Balance: You enter the balance from your paper statement (e.g., $10,000).

  2. Transactions List: You see all posted D365 transactions. You tick the ones that appear on the statement.

  3. Outstanding Items: You leave the $1,000 check un-ticked (Uncleared).

  4. The Logic: D365 performs this internal calculation:

    • Statement Ending Balance ($10,000)

    • Minus Outstanding Checks ($1,000)

    • Equals Calculated Book Balance ($9,000)

If your actual D365 Bank Ledger Balance is $9,000, the "Unreconciled" field at the bottom of the screen will show 0.00. This means you are "balanced," even though the two primary numbers ($10k vs $9k) are different.

4. What Happens Next Month?

When you start the reconciliation for the next month:

  • The check you didn't tick last month automatically carries forward. It will stay in your "Uncleared" list month after month.

  • The moment that check appears on a bank statement (perhaps in April), you simply tick "Cleared" during the April reconciliation.

  • The check then moves from "Outstanding" to "Reconciled," and it will no longer appear in future reconciliation windows.


Do not be tempted to reverse transactions to make the balances match. The reconciliation's job is to document these 'timing differences.' In D365, as long as your Unreconciled amount is zero, your books are correct. The uncleared check remains on the 'Right Side' of the reconciliation worksheet as an outstanding item until the bank statement finally catches up.


But what balance will go to financial statement then?

The balance that appears on your financial statements (Balance Sheet and Trial Balance) is always the General Ledger (GL) Book Balance, not the bank statement balance.

In accounting, your financial statements must reflect the transactions the company has authorized and executed. Here is how that works in practice and why it is the correct approach:

1. The GL Balance is the "Source of Truth"

When you generate a Balance Sheet in Dynamics 365 Finance, the system looks at the Main Account assigned to that bank.

  • Because you posted the check at the end of the month, the ledger has already been credited (reduced).

  • Therefore, your financial statements show the reduced amount.

Example:

  • Bank Statement Balance: $10,000

  • Outstanding Check: $1,000 (Sent to a vendor on the 30th)

  • Balance Sheet (GL) Amount: $9,000

The $9,000 is what goes to your financial statements. This is correct because, from an accounting perspective, you no longer "own" that $1,000; it has been committed to a vendor.

2. Why the Bank Statement Balance is NOT used

If you reported the bank statement balance of $10,000 on your Balance Sheet, you would be overstating your assets. You would be claiming you have $10,000 available to spend, when in reality, $1,000 of that is already promised to a vendor who holds a legal document (the check) to claim it.

3. The Role of the Bank Reconciliation Report

If an auditor or a manager asks, "Why does the Balance Sheet say $9,000 when the bank says we have $10,000?", you provide the Bank Reconciliation Report.

The reconciliation report acts as a "bridge" or a supporting schedule that proves the $9,000 on the financial statement is accurate. It says:

  • "We show $9,000 because we know about a $1,000 check that hasn't reached the bank yet."

4. Summary of the Flow

  1. General Ledger: Tracks every transaction the moment it happens. This balance is used for Financial Reporting.

  2. Bank Statement: Tracks only what the bank has processed.

  3. Bank Reconciliation: A control document used to verify that the difference between the two is legitimate (e.g., outstanding checks, deposits in transit, or bank errors).

Accounting Rule: You report what you know (the Ledger), and you reconcile it to what the external party knows (the Bank).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

There are two types of reconciliation in D365: -

1. Simple Bank Reconciliation (Manual Reconciliation) - User manually reconcile the transactions

2. Advance Bank Reconciliation (Automatic Reconciliation) - System performs the initial reconciliation and at the end when there are transactions which system was not able to reconcile, user reconcile those transactions manually.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this Blog we will see manual reconciliation and in next blogs we will see automatic bank reconciliations

Reference of Microsoft Blog - Reconcile a bank account - Finance | Dynamics 365 | Microsoft Learn

Manual Bank Reconciliation in D365 can be performed with the help of Bank statement provided by the bank.

In the manual bank reconciliation user has to manually reconcile all the transaction by marking them as reconciled and once all the entries are reconciled, they can mark the bank statement as reconciled.

You can't reconcile a bank statement with a bank account if any of the checks or deposit slip payments that the statement lists currently have a status of Pending cancellation. After a reviewer posts or rejects a check reversal or deposit slip payment cancellation, the status isn't Pending cancellation, and you can reconcile the bank account.

  1. Go to Cash and bank management > Bank Accounts > Bank accounts.
    Select the bank account to reconcile with the bank statement and select Reconcile > Account reconciliation.

  2. Enter information in the Bank statement date and Bank statement fields.
    In the Ending balance field, enter the bank account ending balance for the period for which you are doing the reconciliation as per the Bank statement.

  3. Select Transactions to open the Account reconciliation page.

  4. For each transaction that is included on the bank statement, select the Cleared checkbox if the amount in Dynamics 365 Finance corresponds to the amount on the bank statement. 

  5. You can also enter or modify the value in the Bank transaction type field. This field value is important for bank transaction statistics and for some reports.

    Note
    Don't select the Cleared checkbox for transactions that aren't on the bank statement. These transactions continue to be displayed in on this page until they're reconciled with a future bank statement.
    The Cleared checkbox isn't available if the transaction has a status of Pending cancellation. Transactions have this status if Finance requires that reversals or cancellations are reviewed before they're posted. After a reviewer posts or rejects the reversal or cancellation, the status is no longer Pending cancellation, and you can reconcile the bank account with the bank statement.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


To select the Cleared checkbox for an interval of checks that all are displayed on the bank statement, select Mark check interval, and then indicate the interval. If all transactions in the list can be cleared, select Mark all as cleared.


  1. If the amount for a bank account transaction doesn't correspond to the amount for the transaction on the bank statement, enter the amount of the correction in the Correction amount field.

    Note
    If the fiscal period of the transaction to be corrected is closed, you can't use the Correction amount field. Instead, create a line that has a transaction date that is in an open fiscal period for the correction. In this case, you must add the financial dimensions that were used on the original transaction, and also the offset main account.

  2. Create transactions for entries, such as fees and interest, that are on the bank statement but that aren't in Finance. Enter the Bank transaction type and appropriate financial dimensions.

  3. As you mark the transactions on the bank statement as Cleared, the amount in the Unreconciled field, which is recalculated continuously as you make changes, approaches zero. When it reaches zero, select Reconcile account to post the reconciliation, and the transactions and corrections.

    After the reconciliation is posted, the transactions that have been included can't be modified or corrected, and they're not displayed for future account reconciliation.

  4. To view bank transactions that aren't reconciled, use the Unreconciled bank transactions report. To view the bank statement for a bank account, use the Bank statement report.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


Cancel bank statement reconciliation

The Cancel bank statement reconciliation functionality enables you to cancel bank statement reconciliation. You need to enable the Allow bank statement edit parameter. To do this, go to Cash and bank management > Setup > Cash and bank management parameters > Bank reconciliation.


Bank statement reconciliations can only be canceled in the chronological order in which they were entered. When a bank statement reconciliation is canceled, new transactions and corrections are reversed and all other transactions are marked as unreconciled.


To cancel bank statement reconciliation, follow these steps:


Select the bank statement and select Bank statement > Cancel bank reconciliation.

On Cancel bank reconciliation, enter the Reason code, Reason comment, and Cancellation date.

Select OK.
